text: The eleven slides of version 2 are kept word for word as issued, and slides 13 to 21 are the answer of this version: where version 2 says 'the Workbench', 'the orchestrator' or 'the agent platform', version 3 names the service that owns it in the Microservice Ownership Map v1.
why: Rule 1 and Template and Rules R8.2 never edit an existing file or an approved statement, while the realignment must still give every agent step an owner.
read: A reader sees version 2 as issued on slides 3 to 12 and finds the owner of each step on the new slides, without comparing two decks.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, read-me slide 2, and the notes of slides 13 to 21
impact: The deck holds two readings of the same platform in one file; the new slides are the owner statement for the build.

text: Version 3 is issued in Draft. No approval is recorded for this version and the run continues without a human verification stop.
why: The run is a realignment with no approval step (R1 U8) and the source deck carries no approval record.
read: A reader knows the deck may change after review and does not treat it as approved for build.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, read-me slide 2, status line
impact: None on content; the status line changes when approval is recorded.

text: The title slide of version 2 stays slide 1 and the read-me slide is placed second; source slides 2 to 11 therefore sit at positions 3 to 12 and the new slides at 13 to 21, and every page number follows its position.
why: Template and Rules R8.2 keeps the issued deck as it was, and a deck must open on its cover; the page-number boxes are the only text that has to follow the move.
read: No slide of version 2 changes content; only the number in its page-number box changes.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide order and page numbers

text: Version 2 carries no release date. Its document date (28 October 2026 on the title slide) is copied unchanged, and every release date in the programme is tentative (U7, DL48).
why: Rule 10 copies dates unchanged and marks release dates tentative; a date is never raised as a gap.
read: A reader sees the date of the issued deck and knows no release date is committed here.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, title slide and read-me slide 2

text: Every owner in version 3 is a service code P1 to P10 or S1 to S9 of the Ownership Map v1, a platform epic (RWB-PLT-*), or a party outside the 19 services (ACE Common, Enterprise AI, COLLINS). No owner is a team type or a person, and the agent runtime is P10 rwb-agent.
why: R1 U3 makes the owner a suggestion and rule 4 forbids names of people; the Ownership Map is the only owner source of the run.
read: Each step of the deck can be traced to one row of the Ownership Map.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, every table of slides 13 to 21

text: The six parts of source slide 5 (orchestrator, tool gateway, guardrail checker, prompt and policy store, evaluation harness, model endpoint) are all components of rwb-agent (P10), not separate services and not part of the edge.
why: Template and Rules R4 has one row for the agent runtime, Architecture v5 slide 16 puts the workflow, the tool gateway and the rwb_agent tables in one service, and slide 36 lists 'Agent runtime P10 rwb-agent' as reusable as is.
read: A reader finds the whole agent platform inside one deployable, with its own schema, queue and topic.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 14 and 15
impact: A shared gateway or a separate evaluation service would need a new service row.

text: The 60 seconds is the timer of AgentRunWorkflow and covers the whole run, tool reads and guardrail check included; when it fires, the result of the embedded rule package of the step (P7) is used and the fallback is written to the run row.
why: Architecture v5 slide 16 reads 'AgentRunWorkflow: 60 s, then rule result', the NFR line the same, and the workflow is the only timed thing in the run; the rule result of a step is produced by the embedded Drools kit (DP-04).
read: A caller always gets a decision within 60 s and can show whether a person, an agent or a rule produced it.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 16, 17 and 21
impact: If the limit is the model call only, the workflow budget grows and the timer moves inside the activity.

text: A tool call is a REST call on the published contract of the owning service: one hop, 2 s, no new call type. The tool gateway is a component of rwb-agent that holds the workload identity; the agent holds no credential.
why: Source slide 8 makes the gateway the only way an agent reaches data, and ADR-020 with DP-11 fixes the call shape; the source names no other transport.
read: Every read an agent makes appears as a REST call in the trace of the owning service.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 14, 15 and 19
impact: A tool that needs a Temporal or file call would break the rule and needs its own decision.

text: The workflow of the stage service holds the AgentRunWorkflow child handle and passes caseId, step and run number; P10 owns the workflow type, queue rwb-agent and the run history.
why: Architecture v5 gives the stage services an 'Agent: child' step and gives AgentRunWorkflow to P10, and the Ownership Map records P10 as the only owner.
read: A run is visible from the case workflow that started it and from /agent-runs/{id}.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 16 and 21
impact: A different split would move the timer into the caller.

text: The service that owns the stage decision starts the agent run: P5 for intake, S8 for screening and X1 to X7, S1 for valuation and route, S5 for pricing, S2 for settlement and restructure, S3 for the guarantee claim, P8 for reconciliation, S4 for the legal document, S6 for debt sale, S7 for write-off and S8 for the lost customer.
why: Only three runs are drawn on a service contract; for the other nine the stage owner is the only service that holds the decision the agent informs, and leaving them unowned would block their build.
read: Every one of the twelve agents has a calling service and an event path back.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide 18 and slide 21
impact: If a stage moves, the calling service of that agent moves with it.

text: rwb-agent writes its own local decision record in rwb_agent and publishes DecisionRecorded on rwb.decision-record.v1, like every other service; P7 keeps the central ledger.
why: Source slide 8 puts an agent proposal in the decision log on the same terms as a person's, and DP-03 with ADR-022 makes the local record plus the shared topic the pattern for all 19 services.
read: An agent proposal or action is in the ledger within five minutes, with its versions.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 14, 16 and 19

text: The run screen that calls GET /agent-runs/{id} is a gateway-bff composite route to P10 (DP-19), owned by the platform edge epic; the data stays P10's.
why: Every screen call crosses the edge and the Ownership Map has no edge row, so the only place for the route is the platform story that builds it.
read: A person sees a proposal, a fallback and the versions behind it without the service owning a screen.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide 21
impact: The route needs the RWB-PLT-N001-CON story to exist.

text: The six who govern the agents on source slide 10 (strategy and model committee, Model Risk, centre of excellence, Enterprise AI team, risk and model risk officer, internal audit) sit outside the 19 services and are kept unchanged; a policy or prompt change reaches rwb-agent through POST /agent-policies with the authorising role recorded.
why: Governance is a bank function, not a service, and P4 holds roles and authority; the source names no admin role.
read: A reader sees that no service decides its own autonomy or prompt.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide 20 and slide 21
impact: The admin path needs maker-checker before it is opened in production.

text: The evaluation harness keeps its labelled sets and scores in the evaluations table of rwb_agent; no other schema, file or tool is named by a source for them.
why: Source slide 5 names an evaluation harness and Architecture v5 slide 16 lists 'evaluations' among the tables of rwb_agent; nothing else is named.
read: A reader can find the scores behind an autonomy step-up in the service that runs the agent.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 14, 15 and 19
impact: Labelled sets that contain personal data would need the masking rule of P4.

text: Until DL33 is closed, the endpoint of the build is the Enterprise AI private endpoint INT-23, called by rwb-agent only.
why: Source slide 11 leaves DL33 open with an answer used until it is decided, and Architecture v5 names INT-23 as the outside connection of P10.
read: A build has one endpoint and one caller, and the open decision stays visible.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 14 and 21
impact: Closing DL33 on a different endpoint changes the interface contract of P10.

text: The model output of the daily load reaches rwb-agent as a tool read through P1's contract; no service reads the ACE views except P1.
why: ADR-010 and DP-05 give the view read to one service, and Architecture v5 slide 16 lists Source data as P10's tool.
read: A score is read once, by P1, and every consumer sees the same value.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide 13 and slide 21
impact: A score that no view exposes cannot be used until P1 adds it.

text: The autonomy level of a step is configuration, not code: it is a column of the agent policy row in rwb_agent, read by the run and enforced by the rule package of the step from P7.
why: Source slide 9 steps autonomy up on measured results without a release, and DP-04 keeps the rules as data in the owner's embedded kit.
read: A level can be raised or lowered without deploying a service, and every run shows the level it used.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slides 13, 15 and 20
impact: A level change is a policy change and needs the approval path of the committee.

text: The counts of source slide 2 (10 automated, 13 advised, 2 person or partner) hold: every advised decision keeps a person's approval, and L2 to L4 act only inside a band a person has set.
why: Architecture v5 slide 35 says AI never decides, while source slide 9 lets L2 to L4 act; reading the band as a person-set limit keeps both statements true.
read: A reader sees an agent that is faster, never an agent that is unsupervised on a material action.
applied_in: AI and Agent Architecture v3, slide 20 and slide 21
impact: A step at L3 or L4 on a material action would need this reading confirmed first.
